I’m an old hand at this now. Forty years on this land, I don’t do fancy calculating. I look at what worked on my own fields, what the better farmers nearby are doing, and what I can afford without emptying my pocket. My land is only 15 mu and there are just two of us in the house, so I can’t spread myself too thin. This year I’ll keep most of the land in the usual wheat-maize rotation, because that is the steady way here and it gives grain twice. I’ll leave 5 mu in cotton, because cotton still brings cash if the picking goes alright, and I know how to manage it. For wheat, I’ll sow in early October like usual, using the seed sold in town, not the expensive kind. I’ll put base fertilizer before sowing and then topdress once when the wheat starts to pull up in spring. I don’t dare cut fertilizer too much, because if wheat turns yellow, yield drops fast. Water from the well costs money, so I’ll irrigate about three times, mainly at the important stages, not every time the field looks a little dry.

For maize, I’ll plant it right after wheat harvest. That turnaround is always tight, so I won’t do anything slow. I’ll clear the wheat, do light tillage, and seed maize quickly. Maize usually follows the leftover fertility from wheat, so I won’t spend as much on it as on wheat, but I’ll still give it one base dose and one topdress if the stand looks decent. If rain is alright, maybe I irrigate once or twice; if summer rain comes on time, I save that pumping money. Cotton is slower money and takes more hand work, but on 5 mu I can still manage. I’ll plant in late April, use a local improved cotton seed, put fertilizer in two rounds, and water a couple of times if it stays dry. Cotton needs more watching for insects than wheat, so I’ll spray if I see trouble. I’m not chasing the biggest yield. I just want a stable year, enough grain from wheat and maize, and some cash from cotton without spending more than I can bear.
